prompt: An online retailer stores product listings in which each product category has different attributes (shoes have sizes, laptops have CPU and RAM specs). The development team wants to store each product as a single self-describing record and add new attributes without altering a schema. Which database type best fits this requirement?

options.text: Graph database
Document database
Time series database
Relational database with a fixed table per category

explanation: A document database stores each record as a self-describing document (for example JSON or BSON) whose fields can vary from record to record, so new attributes need no schema change. A graph database is optimised for traversing relationships, not varied attribute sets. A time series database is built for timestamped measurements. A relational design with a fixed table per category requires DDL changes every time a category gains an attribute.

prompt: A web application needs to cache user session tokens and look them up by token ID with sub-millisecond latency. No queries other than get, set and delete by ID are required. Which database type is the best fit?

options.text: Key-value store
Column-oriented database
Object-oriented database
Graph database

explanation: A key-value store retrieves an opaque value by its unique key, which is exactly the get/set/delete-by-ID pattern a session cache needs, and in-memory key-value stores give very low latency. A column-oriented database is optimised for analytical scans over a few columns of many rows. An object-oriented database persists programming-language objects with their relationships, which adds overhead with no benefit here. A graph database is built for relationship traversal, not simple lookups.

prompt: A fraud team wants to find accounts that are linked to a known fraudulent account through shared phone numbers, devices or addresses, up to four hops away. Queries against the current relational schema require many self-joins and are slow. Which database type is designed for this kind of query?

options.text: Key-value store
Time series database
Graph database
Document database

explanation: A graph database stores entities as nodes and relationships as edges, so multi-hop traversals such as finding everything within four links of an account are native operations rather than chains of joins. A key-value store can only fetch values by key and has no notion of relationships. A time series database is optimised for timestamped measurements. A document database stores self-contained documents and would still need repeated lookups to follow links.

prompt: A manufacturing company collects temperature and vibration readings from 5,000 sensors every second. Analysts query averages per sensor over time windows, and readings older than 90 days should be downsampled automatically. Which database type is the best fit?

options.text: Object-oriented database
Graph database
Document database
Time series database

explanation: A time series database is optimised for high-volume, append-mostly timestamped data and typically provides time-window aggregation, retention policies and downsampling. An object-oriented database stores application objects and has no special handling of time-ordered measurements. A graph database is built for relationship traversal. A document database can hold the readings but lacks built-in time-based compression, retention and windowed aggregation.

prompt: A company is building a semantic search feature. Text from support articles is converted into embeddings by a machine learning model, and the application must return the articles whose embeddings are most similar to the embedding of a user's question. Which database type is designed for this?

options.text: Vector database
Column-oriented database
Key-value store
Relational database using LIKE predicates

explanation: A vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings and performs nearest-neighbour similarity search (for example using cosine or Euclidean distance) with specialised indexes. A column-oriented database speeds up aggregations over columns but does not provide similarity search. A key-value store can only return a value for an exact key. LIKE predicates match character patterns and cannot measure semantic similarity.

prompt: A data warehouse table has 300 columns and billions of rows. Most reports compute sums and averages over three or four of those columns. Which storage approach reduces the amount of data read from disk for these reports?

options.text: Row-oriented storage with a clustered index on the primary key
Column-oriented storage
Key-value storage keyed by row ID
Document storage with one document per row

explanation: Column-oriented storage keeps each column's values together, so a query touching four of 300 columns reads only those four columns, and similar values compress well. Row-oriented storage with a clustered index still reads whole rows, including the 296 unused columns. Key-value storage by row ID returns whole values per key and is not suited to scans. Document storage with one document per row also reads entire records.

prompt: A development team writes an engineering application in an object-oriented language. They want to persist complex objects, including inheritance hierarchies and references between objects, without translating them into tables and rows. Which database type matches this goal?

options.text: Key-value store
Time series database
Object-oriented database
Column-oriented database

explanation: An object-oriented database stores objects as the application defines them, including inheritance and object references, so no object-to-table mapping is needed. A key-value store holds opaque values by key and does not understand object references. A time series database is specialised for timestamped measurements. A column-oriented database stores tabular data by column for analytics.

prompt: A bank's core ledger requires that a funds transfer debit one account and credit another as a single unit, with strict constraints that prevent orphaned records. Which characteristic makes a relational database the usual choice for this workload?

options.text: It stores data without a schema so new fields can be added at any time
It favours eventual consistency to maximise write availability
It is optimised for traversing relationships between nodes and edges
It enforces a defined schema, referential integrity and ACID transactions

explanation: Relational databases enforce a defined schema, foreign key constraints and ACID transactions, which guarantee the debit and credit either both commit or both roll back. Storing data without a schema describes document stores and removes the constraints a ledger needs. Favouring eventual consistency is a BASE trait common in distributed NoSQL systems and can briefly show inconsistent balances. Node-and-edge traversal describes graph databases.

prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts relational and non-relational databases?

options.text: Relational databases cannot scale beyond one server, while non-relational databases cannot enforce constraints of any kind on stored data
Relational databases store data only as JSON documents, while non-relational databases always use tables
Relational databases use tables with a predefined schema and SQL; non-relational ones use other models with flexible schemas
Relational databases are always open source, while non-relational databases are always proprietary

explanation: Relational databases use tables of rows and columns with a predefined schema and SQL, whereas NoSQL databases use other models (document, key-value, column, graph and so on) and usually allow flexible schemas. Saying relational systems cannot scale beyond one server and NoSQL systems cannot enforce constraints is false; relational systems scale with replicas and sharding, and many NoSQL systems support validation. Relational databases do not store data only as JSON. Licensing is unrelated to the data model; both kinds exist as open source and proprietary products.

prompt: An organisation receives the following data: customer records exported from a CRM into a table with fixed columns, call-centre audio recordings, and JSON event messages whose fields vary slightly between event types. How should these be classified, in that order?

options.text: Structured, unstructured, semistructured
Semistructured, structured, unstructured
Structured, semistructured, unstructured
Unstructured, unstructured, structured

explanation: A table with fixed columns is structured data, audio recordings have no inherent record or field organisation and are unstructured, and JSON with tagged but varying fields is semistructured. The other orderings misplace at least one item: the CRM table has a fixed schema, audio has no field-level structure, and JSON carries self-describing tags without a rigid schema.

prompt: Which of the following is an example of semistructured data?

options.text: A PDF scan of a handwritten form
A table of orders with typed columns and a primary key
An MP4 video file from a security camera
An XML file whose records include different optional elements

explanation: Semistructured data carries its own tags or markers, as XML and JSON do, but does not conform to a rigid table schema, so records can differ. A scanned handwritten form is an image with no machine-readable fields, making it unstructured. A typed table with a primary key is structured. Video files are unstructured.

prompt: A legal firm stores millions of contracts as Word documents and scanned images. Partners want to search the contents and extract clauses. What is the main challenge of this data compared with data in relational tables?

options.text: It is unstructured, so content must be extracted with OCR, full-text indexing or NLP before field-level queries
It is semistructured, so it can be queried directly with standard SQL column predicates
It is structured, so a fixed schema must be designed before any document is stored
It is time series data, so every contract must be stored, indexed and queried strictly in order of its signing timestamp

explanation: Documents and scanned images are unstructured: there are no predefined fields, so content must be extracted through OCR, full-text indexing or NLP before it can be searched by attribute. Calling it semistructured is wrong because the files have no self-describing tags, and even semistructured data is not directly queryable with column predicates. It is not structured because it has no fixed schema. It is not time series data because the records are not timestamped measurements.

prompt: A social media company stores user posts in a wide-column NoSQL database that partitions data across many nodes. During a network partition, users in one region briefly see an older version of a post. What design choice explains this behaviour?

options.text: The database enforces two-phase commit across all nodes before acknowledging writes
The database is relational and runs every transaction at serializable isolation
The database favours availability and eventual consistency, so replicas converge later
The database stores each post as an object within an inheritance hierarchy

explanation: Many distributed NoSQL databases favour availability and accept eventual consistency, so during a partition some replicas can return stale data until they converge. Two-phase commit across nodes would block or fail writes rather than return stale reads. Serializable isolation in a relational database prevents stale reads within a transaction. Object inheritance describes object-oriented databases and has nothing to do with replica staleness.

prompt: A gaming company needs a leaderboard and a shopping-cart service. Both are accessed only by a known identifier, must handle very high request rates, and can tolerate the loss of a few seconds of data if a node fails. Which NoSQL type is the simplest fit?

options.text: Graph database
Key-value store
Vector database
Object-oriented database

explanation: Key-value stores retrieve values by a known key with very high throughput and are commonly used for carts, sessions and leaderboards. A graph database adds relationship traversal that these services do not need. A vector database performs similarity search on embeddings. An object-oriented database persists rich object graphs and is heavier than needed for ID-based lookups.

prompt: Which two workloads are good fits for a document database? (Choose two.)

options.text: A content management system whose articles have varying sections, tags and media metadata
Second-by-second CPU metrics from 10,000 servers with automatic downsampling
A product catalogue where each product type has different attributes
Shortest-path routing between warehouses in a delivery network
Finding the ten images most similar to an uploaded image's embedding

explanation: Records with varying fields, such as CMS articles and heterogeneous product catalogues, suit a document database because each document is self-describing and the schema is flexible. Second-by-second metrics with downsampling are a time series workload. Shortest-path routing is a graph traversal problem. Finding similar images by embedding is a vector similarity search.

prompt: A recommendation engine must answer the question: which products were bought by customers who bought this product, and which of those were bought by the current customer's friends? Which database type models this most naturally?

options.text: Column-oriented database
Time series database
Key-value store
Graph database

explanation: The query follows relationships (customer bought product, customer is a friend of customer), which a graph database stores as edges and traverses efficiently. A column-oriented database is tuned for aggregations over large tables, not relationship hops. A time series database organises data by timestamp. A key-value store returns values by key with no relationship model.

prompt: An IoT team is choosing between a general-purpose relational database and a time series database for storing meter readings. Which capability is a typical advantage of the time series database for this workload?

options.text: Native support for foreign keys and cascading deletes
Built-in retention policies and compression for time-ordered data
Graph traversal of relationships between individual meters
Storage of application objects together with their inheritance

explanation: Time series databases typically compress time-ordered data heavily and provide retention and downsampling policies, which keeps storage manageable for continuous meter readings. Foreign keys with cascading deletes are a relational strength, not a time series one. Graph traversal belongs to graph databases. Storing objects with inheritance is the role of object-oriented databases.

prompt: A team adds an extension to its PostgreSQL database so that it can store embeddings in a column and return rows ordered by distance to a given embedding. Which capability have they added to the relational database?

options.text: Vector similarity search
Key-value caching
Wide-column partitioning
Object-oriented inheritance

explanation: Storing embeddings and ordering results by distance to a query embedding is vector similarity search, which PostgreSQL gains through extensions such as pgvector. Key-value caching is lookup by exact key. Wide-column partitioning distributes rows across nodes by partition key. Object-oriented inheritance concerns modelling class hierarchies, not distance-based search.

prompt: A database administrator must add a loyalty_tier column to the customers table and create an index on it before a new release. Which SQL subtype contains the statements needed for both tasks?

options.text: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
Transaction Control Language (TCL)
Data Definition Language (DDL)
Data Query Language (DQL)

explanation: ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN and CREATE INDEX change database structure, so both are Data Definition Language statements. DML statements such as INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change the rows stored in tables, not their structure. TCL statements such as COMMIT and ROLLBACK control transactions. DQL (SELECT) reads data.

options.text: A, B and C
A and C
Only C
No rows, because a rollback was issued

explanation: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work done after the savepoint, so the insert of B is undone while A remains, and C is inserted afterwards; COMMIT then makes A and C permanent. A, B and C is wrong because B was rolled back. Only C is wrong because the savepoint preserved A. No rows is wrong because rolling back to a savepoint does not end or undo the whole transaction.

prompt:
What does the following query return?

SELECT c.customer_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

options.text: Every customer, once for each order they have placed
Orders that have no matching customer
Only customers who have placed at least one order
Customers who have never placed an order

explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the order columns with NULL where no order matches, and the WHERE o.order_id IS NULL filter keeps only those unmatched customers, an anti-join. Returning every customer once per order would require no filter. Orders without customers would need the join in the other direction. Customers with at least one order are exactly the rows this filter removes.

prompt:
A report must list every customer with their 2025 orders, including customers who placed no orders in 2025. The developer wrote:

SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2025-01-01';

Customers with no 2025 orders are missing from the output. What should the developer change?

options.text: Move the date condition from the WHERE clause into the ON clause of the LEFT JOIN
Change the LEFT JOIN to an INNER JOIN so that only matching order rows are compared
Add DISTINCT to the SELECT list
Replace the LEFT JOIN with a CROSS JOIN

explanation: Filtering a column of the outer-joined table in WHERE discards the NULL-extended rows, which turns the LEFT JOIN into an inner join; putting the date test in the ON clause restricts which orders match while still keeping every customer. Changing to an INNER JOIN would deliberately drop customers without matching orders. DISTINCT removes duplicate rows but cannot restore missing ones. A CROSS JOIN pairs every customer with every order, producing incorrect results.

prompt:
What does the following query return?

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT emp_name, dept_id, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
  FROM employees
) x
WHERE rn = 1;

options.text: The single highest-paid employee in the whole company
One highest-paid employee per department
All employees, numbered from 1 in salary order across the company
The lowest-paid employee in each department

explanation: PARTITION BY dept_id restarts the numbering for each department and ORDER BY salary DESC gives the highest salary row number 1, so filtering on rn = 1 returns one top earner per department. The whole-company answer ignores the partition. Returning all employees ignores the rn = 1 filter. The lowest-paid would require ascending order.

prompt: A department has four employees with salaries 100, 90, 90 and 80. A query ranks them with DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC). What rank does the employee earning 80 receive?
explanation: DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same rank and does not leave gaps, so the ranks are 1, 2, 2 and 3. A rank of 4 is what RANK would return, because RANK skips numbers after a tie. A rank of 2 belongs to the tied 90 salaries. A rank of 1 belongs to the highest salary.

prompt: A finance analyst needs each row of a daily sales table to show the day's amount and a running total of all sales up to and including that day. Which expression produces the running total in a single pass without a self-join?

options.text: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)
SUM(amount) with GROUP BY sale_date
COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY sale_date)
MAX(amount) OVER ()

explanation: A windowed SUM ordered by sale_date accumulates amounts from the first row through the current row by default, producing a running total while keeping every row. SUM with GROUP BY sale_date gives each day's own total, not a cumulative one. COUNT(*) partitioned by date counts rows per day. MAX(amount) OVER () returns the single largest amount on every row.

prompt: A monthly revenue table has one row per month. The analyst wants each row to show the current month's revenue next to the previous month's revenue so the change can be calculated. Which window function should be used?

options.text: NTILE(12) OVER (ORDER BY month_start)
FIRST_VALUE(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start)
RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue)
LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start)

explanation: LAG returns a value from a preceding row in the window order, so LAG(revenue) ordered by month gives the previous month's revenue on each row. NTILE(12) divides rows into 12 buckets. FIRST_VALUE returns the first month's revenue on every row, not the previous month's. RANK orders months by revenue and returns a position, not a prior value.

prompt:
The following query unexpectedly returns no rows, even though many products have never been ordered. The order_items.product_id column allows NULLs and contains some NULL values.

SELECT product_id FROM products
WHERE product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items);

What is the best fix?

options.text: Replace NOT IN with NOT EXISTS using a correlated subquery
Replace NOT IN with IN
Add ORDER BY product_id to the subquery
Change the outer query to SELECT DISTINCT

explanation: When the subquery returns a NULL, x NOT IN (...) evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row, so nothing is returned; NOT EXISTS tests for matching rows and is not affected by NULLs. Replacing NOT IN with IN returns products that have been ordered, the opposite of the requirement. Ordering the subquery has no effect on membership tests. DISTINCT only removes duplicates and cannot make UNKNOWN rows pass the filter.

prompt:
What does the following query return?

SELECT e.emp_name, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(i.salary)
                  FROM employees i
                  WHERE i.dept_id = e.dept_id);

options.text: Employees who earn more than the company-wide average
The average salary of each department
Employees who earn more than the average of their own department
Departments whose average salary exceeds the company average

explanation: The subquery is correlated through i.dept_id = e.dept_id, so it computes the average for each outer row's own department and the outer query keeps employees above that figure. A company-wide comparison would need an uncorrelated subquery without the department condition. The query returns employee rows, not department averages. It does not compare departments against the company average.

prompt:
A developer runs the following query to list customers with more than five orders, and the database returns an error:

SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
GROUP BY customer_id;

What is wrong?

options.text: COUNT(*) cannot be used together with GROUP BY
The GROUP BY clause must come before FROM
customer_id must be wrapped in an aggregate function such as MAX because it is not counted
Aggregate conditions belong in a HAVING clause after GROUP BY, not in WHERE

explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, so it cannot reference an aggregate; the condition must be written as HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 after GROUP BY. COUNT(*) is normally used with GROUP BY. GROUP BY follows FROM and WHERE, not the other way round. customer_id is the grouping column, so it is allowed in the SELECT list without an aggregate.

options.text: Every row in accounts is set to inactive
Only the most recently inserted account is updated
The database rejects the statement because it has no WHERE clause
Only rows whose status was NULL are updated

explanation: An UPDATE without a WHERE clause applies to every row in the table, and with autocommit on the change is committed immediately, so all accounts become inactive. SQL has no concept of updating only the most recent row by default. Standard SQL does not reject an UPDATE that lacks WHERE, although some client tools offer an optional safe-update mode. The statement does not limit itself to NULL values.

prompt: A nightly job opens a cursor over 2 million product rows and, for each row, runs a separate UPDATE that raises the price by 5 percent. The job takes hours. What change follows set-based logic and is most likely to shorten the run?

options.text: Add a COMMIT after every row so locks are released sooner
Replace the loop with a single UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.05 statement
Rewrite the loop in a client-side script that sends each UPDATE over the network
Convert the cursor to a scrollable cursor so rows can be revisited

explanation: Set-based logic lets the database apply one statement to the whole set of rows, avoiding millions of separate statement executions, which is typically far faster than row-by-row processing. Committing after every row adds overhead and still processes rows one at a time. Moving the loop to a client adds network round trips. A scrollable cursor changes navigation, not the row-by-row cost.

prompt: Auditors require that whenever a row's salary value changes in the employees table, the old value, new value, user and timestamp are written to an audit table, regardless of which application makes the change. What should the database developer create?

options.text: A view over employees that hides the salary column
A scheduled job that compares the table each night with the previous day's full backup
An AFTER UPDATE trigger on employees that inserts a row into the audit table
A scalar function that returns the current salary

explanation: An AFTER UPDATE trigger fires inside the database for every qualifying update, whatever the source, and can read the old and new values to write the audit row. A view that hides salary restricts reading but records nothing. A daily comparison with a backup misses intermediate changes and cannot identify who made them. A scalar function returns values when called and does not react to changes.

prompt: A view joins customers and addresses. The application must be able to insert through the view, but the database cannot update a multi-table view directly. Which object lets the developer define how inserts against the view are applied to the underlying tables?

options.text: An INSTEAD OF INSERT trigger on the view
A BEFORE INSERT trigger on the customers table
A CHECK constraint on the view
A table-valued function that selects from the view

explanation: An INSTEAD OF trigger on a view runs in place of the attempted insert and can write the appropriate rows to each base table. A BEFORE INSERT trigger on customers fires only for inserts on that table, not on the view. A CHECK constraint validates values but cannot redirect an insert. A table-valued function returns rows and does not handle inserts.

prompt: An order-entry process validates stock, inserts an order header, inserts order lines and updates inventory. The DBA wants applications to run this logic with one call, wants users to be able to run it without direct INSERT or UPDATE rights on the tables, and wants inputs passed as parameters. What should be created?

options.text: A view that joins orders, order lines and inventory with WITH CHECK OPTION
A stored procedure that performs the steps in a transaction
A computed column on the orders table
A nonclustered index on the inventory table

explanation: A stored procedure encapsulates multi-step logic, accepts parameters and can be run by users who are granted EXECUTE on it without holding rights on the underlying tables. A view presents a query result and cannot run a sequence of inserts and updates. A computed column derives a value within a row. An index speeds lookups but contains no logic.

prompt: Several reports calculate a shipping charge from weight and destination zone using the same formula. The developer wants to call the calculation directly in the SELECT list of many queries, for example SELECT order_id, shipping_cost(weight, zone) FROM orders. What should be created?

options.text: A trigger on the orders table
A stored procedure that prints the cost
A user-defined scalar function
A savepoint inside each report

explanation: A user-defined scalar function takes parameters, returns a single value and can be used inside expressions such as a SELECT list. A trigger runs in response to data changes and cannot be called from a query. A stored procedure is invoked with CALL or EXEC and generally cannot be used inside a SELECT list expression. A savepoint marks a point within a transaction and performs no calculation.

prompt: Which two statements are Data Manipulation Language (DML)? (Choose two.)

options.text: CREATE TABLE
DELETE
GRANT
INSERT
COMMIT

explanation: DELETE and INSERT change the rows stored in a table, which makes them DML. CREATE TABLE defines structure and is DDL. GRANT assigns permissions and belongs to Data Control Language. COMMIT ends a transaction and is Transaction Control Language.

prompt: A DBA runs a weekly index-maintenance script from a laptop. The job fails whenever the laptop is asleep or off the VPN. Where should the script run so that it is reliable and close to the data?

options.text: On the database server or a job server, started by a scheduler such as cron or a job agent
In the web browser of whichever analyst is logged on
On the DBA's laptop, with power settings changed so it stays awake and connected to the VPN overnight
Inside the client application each time a user signs in

explanation: A server-side script started by a scheduler runs whether or not any workstation is available and avoids moving data across the network. Running it in an analyst's browser makes it depend on a user session and client resources. Keeping the laptop awake still depends on one device and its VPN link. Running maintenance whenever a user signs in would repeat heavy work unpredictably during business hours.

prompt: A web form uses client-side JavaScript to reject order quantities below 1 before submitting. A developer proposes removing the equivalent check from the database because the browser already enforces it. Why is this a bad idea?

options.text: Client-side scripts run on the server and therefore duplicate the database check
Client-side JavaScript cannot read the values typed into a form field
Browsers block JavaScript validation by default
Client-side checks can be bypassed, so the rule must also be enforced on the server or database

explanation: Client-side scripts run on the user's device and can be disabled or bypassed by sending requests directly, so server-side or database constraints remain necessary for integrity. Client-side scripts do not run on the server. JavaScript can read form values, which is how such validation works. Browsers run JavaScript by default.

prompt: A Windows-based team manages 40 SQL Server instances and wants to automate checking job status and running T-SQL scripts on each server from one scheduled script, using a Microsoft-supported module. Which scripting language fits best?

options.text: Perl with a regular expression module
PowerShell with the SqlServer module
Unix shell with awk
Client-side JavaScript

explanation: PowerShell is Microsoft's automation shell, and the SqlServer module provides cmdlets such as Invoke-Sqlcmd for running queries against many instances from one script. Perl can connect to databases but is not the Microsoft-supported tool for this environment. A Unix shell with awk is a text-processing approach not native to these Windows servers. Client-side JavaScript runs in a browser and cannot manage servers.

prompt: A DBA copies a PowerShell maintenance script to a new Windows server. Running it fails with an error that running scripts is disabled on this system. What should the DBA address?

options.text: The script must be renamed with a .bat extension
The SQL Server service account lacks the sysadmin role
The PowerShell execution policy, for example by signing the script or applying an approved policy
PowerShell can only run scripts stored on network shares, so the file must be moved to a UNC path first

explanation: This message comes from the PowerShell execution policy, which controls whether scripts can run; signing the script or applying the organisation's approved policy resolves it. Renaming to .bat would hand the file to cmd.exe, which cannot run PowerShell syntax. A database role does not stop PowerShell from loading a script. PowerShell runs local scripts when the policy allows them.

prompt: A data engineer needs to pull data from PostgreSQL, clean and reshape it with DataFrames, and write the result back to another database, all in one script that analysts can also read and maintain. Which language is the most common choice for this?

options.text: Unix shell
Perl
PowerShell
Python

explanation: Python has mature database drivers (such as psycopg for PostgreSQL) and data libraries such as pandas for DataFrame-based cleaning, making it the usual choice for this kind of pipeline. A Unix shell is good for orchestrating commands but has no DataFrame library. Perl handles text processing and has database access through DBI but lacks a comparable DataFrame ecosystem. PowerShell can query databases but is not the common choice for DataFrame-based transformation.

prompt: A Python ETL script works on a developer's machine but fails on the production server because a different version of the database driver library is installed there. What practice prevents this?

options.text: Run the script with administrator rights on the server
Use a virtual environment with pinned dependency versions in a requirements file
Convert the script to a Unix shell script
Store the script inside the database as a BLOB

explanation: A virtual environment isolates the script's packages, and a requirements file with pinned versions installs the same library versions in every environment. Administrator rights do not change which library version is installed. Rewriting in shell discards the Python logic without solving dependency management. Storing the script as a BLOB does not control its runtime libraries.

prompt:
A Linux DBA adds the following line to the crontab of the postgres user:

0 2 * * * /opt/scripts/nightly_dump.sh

When does the script run?

options.text: Every day at 02:00
Every two minutes
At midnight on the second day of every month
Every Sunday at 02:00

explanation: Cron fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, so 0 2 * * * means minute 0 of hour 2 on every day. Every two minutes would be */2 in the minute field. Midnight on the second day of each month would be 0 0 2 * *. Sundays only would need a 0 or 7 in the day-of-week field.

prompt: A Bash backup script runs pg_dump, copies the file off-site and then deletes backups older than seven days. One night pg_dump failed, but the script still deleted old backups and reported success. What change should be made?

options.text: Launch the script with nohup so it keeps running even after the session that scheduled it logs out
Replace pg_dump with a SELECT * query
Change the shebang line to use the C shell
Check each command's exit status, with set -e or by testing $?, and stop before cleanup on failure

explanation: Bash continues after a failing command unless the script checks exit codes, so using set -e or testing $? after pg_dump stops the cleanup when the dump fails. nohup only keeps a process alive after logout. A SELECT * query does not produce a restorable backup. Switching to the C shell does not by itself add error handling.

prompt: A company maintains a legacy Perl script that connects to several database products using the same DBI calls. The team needs it to connect to a new PostgreSQL server. What must be installed alongside DBI?

options.text: The PostgreSQL JDBC driver
The psql command-line client only
The DBD::Pg database driver module
An ODBC driver for SQL Server

explanation: Perl's DBI is a database-independent interface that relies on a DBD driver module for each product, and DBD::Pg is the driver for PostgreSQL. A JDBC driver is for Java applications. The psql client alone does not give DBI a driver. A SQL Server ODBC driver targets a different product.

prompt: A shell script connects to PostgreSQL with psql every night. The DBA does not want the password on the command line or in the script. Which approach is supported by psql?

options.text: Embed the password in the script's file name
Store the credentials in a .pgpass file owned by the service account and readable only by it
Pass the password as the first positional argument to psql so it never appears in the script body
Put the password in a comment on the first line of the script

explanation: psql reads passwords from a .pgpass file in the user's home directory and, on Unix, ignores the file if its permissions are more permissive than owner read/write, which keeps the password out of scripts and process lists. A file name is visible to anyone who can list the directory. psql does not take a password as a positional argument; positional arguments are the database and user names. A comment in the script is not read by psql and exposes the password.

prompt: A DBA needs to run a 300-line migration .sql file from a scheduled task on a headless Linux server and capture the output in a log. Which approach fits?

options.text: Open the file in a graphical IDE on the server console, press Run and copy the output pane into a log file
Paste the statements into a web-based query editor and save the results page as the log
Use a command-line client such as psql -f migration.sql and redirect output to a log file
Convert the file into a spreadsheet macro

explanation: Command-line clients run script files non-interactively, can be launched by schedulers and allow output redirection, which suits headless automation. A graphical IDE needs a desktop session and a person to run it. A web query editor is interactive and not scriptable from a scheduler. A spreadsheet macro is not a database scripting tool.

prompt: A new developer is writing complex stored procedures and wants code completion, syntax highlighting, a visual execution plan and step-through debugging. Which environment provides these?

options.text: A database IDE such as DBeaver, SSMS or VS Code with database extensions
A plain command-line client run in a terminal
A cron table on the database server
A flat-file editor with no database connection

explanation: Database IDEs combine an editor with code completion, syntax highlighting, graphical execution plans and, for supported products, debugging. A plain command-line client runs statements but lacks graphical plans and code completion. A cron table only schedules commands. An editor with no database connection cannot show plans or run code.

prompt: Which two are advantages of command-line scripting over working interactively in an IDE? (Choose two.)

options.text: Scripts can be scheduled and run unattended
Graphical execution plans are displayed automatically
The same script can be version-controlled and repeated identically across environments
Drag-and-drop table designers are available
Code completion suggests column names as you type

explanation: Command-line scripts can be scheduled to run without a person and, being plain files, can be version-controlled and replayed identically in each environment. Graphical execution plans, drag-and-drop designers and code completion are features of IDEs, not of command-line scripting.

prompt: An application on a branch-office network issues about 200 small queries to build each page, and page loads are slow because of WAN latency. Moving which logic to the server side would most reduce the round trips?

options.text: Moving the page layout code into the database
Moving the data-assembly logic into a stored procedure that returns the needed result sets in one call
Moving the queries into a client-side script that runs in each user's browser and calls the database directly
Moving the database to the branch office's file share

explanation: A stored procedure runs on the database server, so the many small queries execute locally and the client makes one round trip to receive the results. Page layout is presentation logic and does not belong in the database. Moving the queries into the browser leaves every round trip in place. A file share is not a database server and cannot serve queries.

prompt: Which feature distinguishes PowerShell pipelines from traditional Unix shell pipelines?

options.text: PowerShell pipelines can only run on Windows Server Core installations, while Unix pipelines run anywhere
PowerShell does not support piping between commands
PowerShell passes structured .NET objects between commands, whereas Unix shells pass text streams
Unix shells pass compiled binaries between commands

explanation: PowerShell cmdlets emit objects with properties, so the next command can work with fields directly, while Unix shells pass plain text that is parsed with tools such as awk or cut. PowerShell 7 runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, not only Server Core. PowerShell fully supports pipelines. Unix pipelines carry byte streams, not binaries.

prompt: An analyst's client-side Python script downloads 20 million order rows every morning to compute totals per region on a laptop. The download takes 40 minutes. What change best uses the runtime location of each component?

options.text: Upgrade the laptop's memory and keep the script as is
Export the whole table nightly to a CSV file on a network file share and have the script read it from there
Run the script twice in parallel
Push the aggregation to the server with a GROUP BY query so only the regional totals are returned

explanation: Doing the aggregation in the database, close to the data, returns only a few summary rows instead of transferring 20 million. More laptop memory does not shorten the network transfer. Copying to a CSV on a share still moves all the rows. Running the script twice doubles the load.

prompt: A team has hundreds of text log files from database servers and needs a quick script that uses regular expressions to extract error codes and timestamps. An existing toolkit in the company already does similar work in Perl. Why is Perl a reasonable choice here?

options.text: Perl has strong built-in regular expression and text-processing support
Perl is the only language that can open text files
Perl runs only inside the database engine
Perl scripts are compiled into stored procedures automatically

explanation: Perl was designed with built-in regular expressions and text processing, which makes log parsing straightforward and fits the existing toolkit. Many languages can open text files, so that is not a distinguishing reason. Perl runs as an external interpreter, not inside the database engine. Perl scripts are not converted into stored procedures.

prompt: A Linux administrator writes a maintenance script named rotate_logs.sh and runs it as ./rotate_logs.sh, but receives a permission denied error even though the file is readable. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Rename the file with a .ps1 extension
Grant the execute permission with chmod +x rotate_logs.sh
Move the file into the database data directory
Add a GRANT EXECUTE statement for the file in SQL

explanation: Running a script directly on Linux requires the execute bit, which chmod +x sets; without it the shell reports permission denied. A .ps1 extension is for PowerShell and does not change file permissions. Moving the file into the data directory does not add execute permission and puts clutter beside database files. SQL GRANT EXECUTE applies to database objects such as procedures, not operating system files.

prompt:
After enabling SQL logging for a Java application that uses Hibernate, a DBA sees this pattern for a single page request:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date = ?
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ?
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ?
... (repeated 500 times with different ids)

What problem does this show, and what is the usual remediation?

options.text: A missing primary key on orders; add one
An N+1 query problem from lazy loading; fetch customers with the orders by join fetch or batch fetching
A deadlock between two sessions; lower the isolation level so each lookup releases its shared locks sooner
SQL injection through the id parameter; escape or validate the input before it is concatenated into each query

explanation: One query for the parent rows followed by one query per row for related data is the N+1 pattern that lazy loading produces, and a join fetch or batch fetching loads the customers in one or a few queries. A missing primary key would not cause repeated per-row lookups. A deadlock causes an error and rollback, not hundreds of successful selects. The statements use bind parameters (?), which is the opposite of an injection pattern.

prompt: A DBA wants to review the SQL that Hibernate generates in a development environment. Which setting makes Hibernate print the SQL statements it executes?

options.text: hibernate.show_sql=true
echo=True in create_engine
LogTo(Console.WriteLine) in OnConfiguring
dbt compile --select model

explanation: Setting hibernate.show_sql to true (or enabling the org.hibernate.SQL logger) makes Hibernate output the SQL it sends to the database. echo=True on create_engine is the SQLAlchemy equivalent. LogTo in OnConfiguring is how Entity Framework Core logs. dbt compile renders dbt models to SQL and has nothing to do with Hibernate.

prompt: A .NET team using Entity Framework Core suspects a LINQ query is generating inefficient SQL. How can they see the SQL that EF Core sends to the database?

options.text: Set hibernate.show_sql in the application properties
Enable the io.ebean.SQL logger
Open the target/compiled folder produced by dbt
Configure the DbContext with LogTo so executed commands are written to a log

explanation: EF Core's simple logging, configured by calling LogTo on the DbContext options, writes each executed command and its SQL to the chosen output. hibernate.show_sql is a Hibernate property. io.ebean.SQL is Ebean's SQL logger. The dbt target folder holds compiled dbt models, not EF Core queries.

prompt: A Python service uses SQLAlchemy. During testing, a developer wants every SQL statement the engine emits to be printed so it can be reviewed with the DBA. What is the simplest way?

options.text: Add hibernate.format_sql=true
Pass echo=True when calling create_engine
Run dbt run --full-refresh
Set the database's max_connections to 1

explanation: Creating the SQLAlchemy engine with echo=True logs all SQL statements it emits, which is a quick way to review generated SQL. hibernate.format_sql is a Hibernate property. dbt run --full-refresh rebuilds dbt incremental models. Limiting max_connections changes server capacity and does not reveal SQL.

prompt: A Java team uses the Ebean ORM and wants to see the SQL statements and bind values it executes so they can look for slow queries. What should they enable?

options.text: The io.ebean.SQL logger at debug level
SQL Server Agent alerts
The EF Core EnableSensitiveDataLogging option
The SQLAlchemy echo flag

explanation: Ebean logs executed SQL and bind values through the io.ebean.SQL logger, so enabling it at debug level shows the generated statements. SQL Server Agent alerts notify on job or error events and do not show ORM SQL. EnableSensitiveDataLogging is an EF Core option. The echo flag belongs to SQLAlchemy.

prompt: An analytics engineer has changed a dbt model that uses Jinja and ref() calls. Before running it against the production warehouse, the DBA wants to read the exact SQL that will execute. What should the engineer do?

options.text: Run the model in production and read the warehouse query history
Read the model's .sql source file, because dbt sends it unchanged
Run dbt compile and review the rendered SQL it writes under the target directory
Enable Hibernate SQL logging on the warehouse

explanation: dbt compile renders Jinja and ref() calls into plain SQL and writes it to the target directory without executing it, so it can be reviewed first. Running in production defeats the purpose of reviewing beforehand. The source file contains templating that dbt resolves, so it is not the SQL that runs. Hibernate is a Java ORM and is unrelated to dbt.

prompt: A dbt model that joins several large tables is materialised as a view. Dashboards that query it are slow because the joins run every time the view is read. Which change addresses this?

options.text: Change the model's materialisation to table or incremental so results are stored
Change the materialisation to ephemeral so the model is inlined into each downstream query
Remove ref() calls and hard-code table names
Add a SQLAlchemy engine to the dashboard

explanation: A view reruns its query on every read, whereas a table or incremental materialisation stores the results so dashboards read precomputed data. Ephemeral models are inlined as CTEs into downstream models and are not stored at all. Hard-coding table names breaks dependency tracking and does not change performance. Adding SQLAlchemy to the dashboard does not change how the model is materialised.

options.text: Add an index on image_blob
Increase the connection pool size
Change the query to a projection that selects only the columns the page needs
Wrap the query in a transaction with serializable isolation

explanation: Loading full entities pulls large BLOB columns that the page never uses; projecting only id, name and price cuts I/O and network transfer. Indexing a BLOB column does nothing for a query with no filter. A larger pool adds concurrency but each query still transfers the BLOBs. Serializable isolation adds locking overhead and does not reduce the data returned.

options.text: Bind parameters always force table scans because the value is unknown at compile time; use literals
The function on the column stops the plain index being used; add an index on LOWER(email)
SELECT * always forces a full table scan; list only the needed columns explicitly instead
The table needs a trigger that lowercases the query

explanation: Wrapping the indexed column in LOWER() means the index on the raw email value cannot be used for the comparison, so the optimiser scans; an expression (function-based) index or a normalised stored column restores index access. Bind parameters do not force scans and are preferred over literals. Listing columns reduces data returned but does not change the scan caused by the predicate. Triggers act on data changes and cannot alter a query's predicate.

prompt: An application needs the 20 open tickets for one customer. The DBA sees that the ORM is issuing SELECT * FROM tickets with no WHERE clause, returning 3 million rows, and the code then filters the list in application memory. What should be done?

options.text: Increase the database server's memory
Add more application servers behind the load balancer to share the in-memory filtering
Schedule the query to run only overnight and cache the full result on the application server
Rewrite the ORM query so the filter becomes a WHERE clause run by the database

explanation: The filter is being evaluated in the application after the whole table has been fetched; expressing it so the ORM translates it into SQL lets the database return only the 20 rows. More database memory does not stop 3 million rows being sent. More application servers multiply the problem. Running only at night breaks an interactive feature.

options.text: Skipped rows are still read and discarded; use keyset pagination (WHERE event_id > last_id)
LIMIT is not supported with ORDER BY; remove ORDER BY
The OFFSET value exceeds the integer range supported by LIMIT, so it must be cast to BIGINT
The query is missing a GROUP BY; group by event_id

explanation: With a large OFFSET the database must produce and throw away all the earlier rows, so cost grows with the page number; keyset pagination seeks directly past the last key seen using the index. LIMIT works with ORDER BY and needs it for stable pages. 200,000 is well within the integer range. GROUP BY would not change the cost and is not needed.

prompt: On SQL Server, an ORM sends a parameter typed as nvarchar for a lookup against a varchar column with an index. The plan shows an index scan with an implicit conversion warning instead of a seek. What is the best remediation?

options.text: Drop the index because it is not being used
Configure the ORM mapping so the parameter type matches the column's varchar type
Add a NOLOCK table hint so the scan does not wait on shared locks
Add a second, identical nonclustered index on the column to give the optimiser a choice

explanation: When the parameter's data type has higher precedence than the column's, SQL Server converts the column values, which can prevent an index seek; mapping the parameter to varchar lets the index be used. Dropping the index removes the fix rather than enabling it. NOLOCK changes locking behaviour, not type conversion. A duplicate index suffers the same conversion problem.

prompt: A team is upgrading its ORM version. Which two steps best determine the upgrade's impact on the database server before it reaches production? (Choose two.)

options.text: Deploy to production and wait for user complaints
Disable all database logging to reduce overhead during the test
Rely on the ORM's release notes alone
Run a representative workload in a test environment with production-like data volumes
Compare captured SQL, execution plans and metrics such as CPU, reads and duration before and after the upgrade

explanation: Running a representative workload on production-like data and comparing generated SQL, plans and resource metrics before and after the change measures the real impact. Waiting for user complaints finds problems only after they hurt users. Disabling logging removes the evidence needed to compare. Release notes rarely describe every change to generated SQL for a given application.

prompt:
A report built with an ORM suddenly returns far more rows than expected. The DBA captures the generated SQL:

SELECT o.order_id, p.product_name
FROM orders o, products p
WHERE o.order_date = '2025-06-01';

What is wrong with this code?

options.text: The date literal must use double quotes
Comma-separated tables are not valid SQL
There is no join condition between orders and products, producing a Cartesian product
The SELECT list must include every column of both tables whenever two tables are listed in FROM

explanation: Listing two tables without a join predicate pairs every matching order with every product, a Cartesian product, which multiplies the row count; the mapping must add a condition through the order-lines relationship. In standard SQL, string and date literals use single quotes; double quotes delimit identifiers. Comma-separated FROM lists are valid SQL, they just need a join condition in WHERE. Selecting every column is not required.

prompt: An import routine using an ORM saves 50,000 new records by calling save and commit inside a loop, one record at a time. The database shows high transaction log activity and the import takes an hour. Which remediation is most appropriate?

options.text: Add an index to every column of the target table
Switch the database to a binary collation so string comparisons during each insert are cheaper
Run the loop on two parallel threads, keeping the same per-row save and commit calls on each
Enable batched inserts and commit in larger units of work, or use a bulk-load facility

explanation: Per-row commits force a log flush and round trip for every record; batching statements and committing in larger units of work, or using a bulk-load tool, greatly reduces this overhead. Indexing every column slows inserts further. Collation affects sorting and comparison, not insert speed. Two threads with per-row commits still pay the per-commit cost and can add contention.

prompt: A complex month-end report generated through an ORM produces a deeply nested query that the optimiser handles poorly, and tuning the ORM mapping has not helped. What is a reasonable remediation?

options.text: Rewrite the report as hand-written SQL, a view or a stored procedure called by the app
Increase the ORM's lazy-loading depth so related entities are fetched as the report needs them
Run the report against the transaction log
Disable the database's query optimiser

explanation: When an ORM cannot express a query efficiently, hand-written SQL, a view or a stored procedure lets the DBA control the statement and tune it directly. Increasing lazy-loading depth issues more queries rather than better ones. The transaction log is not a reporting source. The optimiser cannot be disabled in mainstream databases and disabling it would make performance worse.

prompt: A DBA notices thousands of nearly identical statements in the plan cache that differ only in a literal customer ID, each compiled separately. The statements come from code that builds SQL strings by concatenating values. What change improves plan reuse and also reduces security risk?

options.text: Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) to every statement
Increase the size of the plan cache
Use parameterised queries (bind variables) in the ORM or data-access code
Store the customer IDs in a temporary table and join to it from each concatenated statement

explanation: Parameterised queries send one statement text with bind values, so the database can reuse a cached plan, and they prevent SQL injection through concatenated input. Forcing recompilation on every statement increases CPU use. A larger cache stores more single-use plans without fixing the cause. A temporary table does not address how the statements are built.

prompt: An EF Core query loads blogs with two collection navigations, posts and contributors, using Include. The generated single SQL statement returns a very large result because every post row is repeated for every contributor. Which EF Core feature is intended to remediate this?

options.text: Disabling change tracking globally so that fewer entity instances are materialised in memory
Using split queries (AsSplitQuery) so each collection is loaded by a separate SQL statement
Calling LogTo to write the query to a file
Switching the EF Core provider to a NoSQL document database so collections are embedded

explanation: Including several collections in one joined query causes a cartesian explosion of rows, and EF Core's split queries load each collection with its own SQL statement to avoid that duplication. Disabling change tracking reduces memory overhead for tracked entities but does not change the join shape. LogTo only records the SQL. Switching to a NoSQL provider is a major redesign, not a remediation of the query.

prompt: Before replacing a departmental database, a project team documents what the current system provides, lists what the business now requires, and identifies the missing capabilities that the new system must supply. Which requirements-gathering activity is this?

options.text: Stress testing
Regression testing
Data mapping
Gap analysis

explanation: Gap analysis compares the current state with the desired state to identify what is missing. Stress testing pushes a system beyond normal load to find its limits. Regression testing checks that existing functionality still works after a change. Data mapping matches source fields to target fields during a migration or import.

prompt: A database is 200 GB today and has grown by a steady 15 GB per month. The hardware being purchased must last three years without a storage upgrade. Using simple linear projection, what is the minimum data size the team should plan for, before adding headroom for indexes, logs and backups?

options.text: About 245 GB
About 740 GB
About 380 GB
About 1,080 GB

explanation: Thirty-six months at 15 GB per month adds 540 GB, so 200 GB grows to about 740 GB, before headroom. About 245 GB covers only three months of growth. About 380 GB covers only one year. About 1,080 GB assumes 30 GB per month, double the observed rate.

prompt: An order-processing database performs thousands of small random reads and writes per second and has a strict latency target. Which storage choice best matches this requirement?

options.text: Solid-state storage sized for the required IOPS and low latency
High-capacity spinning disks optimised for sequential throughput and cost per gigabyte
Object storage accessed over HTTPS
A tape library with a disk cache

explanation: Random small-block I/O with tight latency targets needs high IOPS, which solid-state storage delivers far better than spinning disks. High-capacity spinning disks suit sequential workloads such as archives but have high random-access latency. Object storage is accessed through an API and is not suited to database data files. Tape is a sequential archival medium.

prompt: A team is planning storage for a self-managed database on cloud virtual machines. Data files need low-latency random access from one server, and monthly backup files must be kept cheaply for seven years. Which combination is most appropriate?

options.text: Object storage for the data files and block storage for the backups
Shared file storage for the data files and the virtual machine's temporary disk for the backups
Block storage volumes for the data files and object storage with an archive tier for the backups
Object storage for both, accessed through a REST API from the database engine

explanation: Block volumes behave like local disks and give the low-latency random I/O database files need, while object storage with an archive tier is inexpensive for long-term backup retention. Putting data files on object storage gives the wrong access pattern, and block storage is a costly place for seven-year archives. A VM's temporary disk can be lost when the VM is moved or stopped. Database engines do not normally run their data files over a REST object API.

prompt: A hospital must keep its patient database in its own data centre for regulatory reasons, but wants to use cloud compute for large, anonymised research reports that run a few times a month. Which deployment model fits?

options.text: Fully on-premises, with research reports run on the production server
Fully cloud-based, moving the patient database to a public cloud region with encryption enabled
Software as a service for the patient database
Hybrid: the regulated database on-premises, anonymised reporting in the cloud

explanation: A hybrid model keeps regulated data on-premises while using cloud capacity for workloads that can run there, such as anonymised reporting. Running heavy research reports on the production server adds load to a critical system and gives no elastic capacity. Moving the patient database to the cloud contradicts the requirement to keep it in the hospital's data centre. Replacing it with a SaaS product also moves the regulated data to a provider.

prompt: A new customer portal is expected to have 50,000 registered users, of whom about 2,000 will be active at peak. The database server's maximum connection setting is 500. Which planning conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Use connection pooling sized for peak concurrency, not one connection per registered user
Set the maximum connection limit to 50,000 so every registered user has a connection
Block new registrations once 500 users have signed up
Ignore the user numbers, because idle connection counts do not materially affect database server resources

explanation: Capacity planning should be based on concurrent users, and connection pooling lets many application requests share a manageable number of database connections. Allowing 50,000 connections would waste memory, because each connection consumes server resources. Limiting registrations to 500 confuses registered users with concurrent connections. Connection counts do affect memory and CPU, so they cannot be ignored.

prompt: An application has two groups of users: call-centre agents running short transactions all day, and finance analysts who run long aggregate queries at month-end. Agents complain that the system slows during month-end. Which design choice best addresses the different user types?

options.text: Give analysts the same short timeout as agents so their queries are cancelled
Route analyst reporting to a read replica or separate reporting database
Disable indexes during month-end to speed up writes
Move the agents to a nightly batch process

explanation: Separating analytical reads onto a replica or reporting database keeps long aggregate queries from competing with short transactions. Cancelling analysts' queries stops them doing their work. Disabling indexes would slow the agents' lookups. Moving agents to a nightly batch breaks the real-time call-centre process.

prompt: An SLA for a database service specifies 99.9 percent availability per year as a key performance indicator. Approximately how much unplanned downtime per year does this allow?

options.text: About 52 minutes
About 87.6 hours
About 8.76 hours
About 5 minutes

explanation: A year has 8,760 hours, and 0.1 percent of that is about 8.76 hours of permitted downtime. About 52 minutes corresponds to 99.99 percent. About 87.6 hours corresponds to 99 percent. About 5 minutes corresponds to 99.999 percent.

prompt: A database SLA states that a severity-1 outage must be acknowledged within 15 minutes and, if not resolved within one hour, referred to the vendor's senior engineers and the customer's service manager. Which part of the SLA does the second requirement describe?

options.text: A key performance indicator for throughput
The reporting schedule for monthly availability statistics
The recovery point objective for backups
An escalation procedure

explanation: An escalation procedure defines who an unresolved issue is passed to, and when, as severity or elapsed time increases. A throughput KPI measures work done per unit of time. The reporting schedule covers how and when SLA performance is reported. A recovery point objective defines acceptable data loss, not who is contacted.

prompt: A DBA is about to install a database engine on a new Linux server. Which activity belongs to checking database prerequisites before installation?

options.text: Verifying the supported OS version, required packages, kernel settings and service account
Creating application tables and loading production data
Running regression tests against the application
Configuring log shipping from the new server to the disaster recovery site and testing the first restore

explanation: Prerequisites are the conditions the engine needs before it can be installed, such as a supported OS release, dependent packages, kernel settings and a service account. Creating tables and loading data happen after installation. Regression testing follows application changes. Log shipping is configured once the database exists.

prompt: A team needs to create identical development, test and production database servers, with the same storage layout, parameters and accounts, and wants to rebuild them quickly when needed. Which approach to provisioning best meets this goal?

options.text: Build each server by hand using a checklist
Clone the production server's disk image, including its data, onto each developer's laptop and test server
Define the servers as infrastructure as code templates and provision them from those definitions
Order physical servers in advance and leave them unconfigured

explanation: Infrastructure as code templates describe the resources and settings once and provision them identically and repeatably. Manual builds from a checklist tend to drift and take longer. Cloning production images to laptops spreads production data and does not create proper servers. Unconfigured hardware does not provision anything.

prompt: A company must upgrade its database engine by a major version. Which plan best reduces the risk of the upgrade?

options.text: Upgrade production first because it has the most realistic data
Upgrade directly on production during business hours so that staff are available, and roll forward if problems occur
Skip backups because the upgrade tool preserves data files
Review deprecated features, rehearse on a production copy, take a verified backup and plan rollback

explanation: Reviewing deprecated or changed features, rehearsing on a production copy, taking a verified backup and planning rollback reduces both the chance and the impact of failure. Upgrading production first or during business hours exposes users to untested changes. Skipping backups leaves no recovery path if the upgrade corrupts data or must be reversed.

prompt: A DBA is importing customers and orders from CSV files into tables where orders.customer_id has a foreign key to customers. The order import keeps failing with foreign key violations. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: Orders are being loaded before their customers; load the parent customers table first
The CSV files use commas; convert them to tab-separated files
The orders table needs a clustered index on order_date before rows can be validated against customers
The foreign key must be changed into a CHECK constraint

explanation: A child row cannot reference a parent that does not exist yet, so the parent table must be imported first. The delimiter does not cause foreign key errors. An index on order_date has no effect on referential integrity. A CHECK constraint cannot verify that a value exists in another table, so it would remove the integrity guarantee.

prompt: A vendor's monitoring agent must be installed on the database server's operating system, and the DBA needs to control OS patching and the exact database engine version. Which cloud service model is required?

options.text: Software as a service (SaaS)
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
Database as a service (DBaaS)
Platform as a service (PaaS) for web applications

explanation: IaaS provides virtual machines on which the customer controls the OS and installs and manages the database software. SaaS delivers a finished application with no access to its database server. DBaaS manages the OS and engine for the customer and does not allow installing agents on the host. A web-application PaaS manages the platform and hides the OS.

prompt: A small company wants a relational database without patching the OS or engine, handling backups or configuring high availability, while still writing its own schemas and SQL. Which service model fits best?

options.text: Infrastructure as a service with a self-installed engine
On-premises servers in a co-location facility
Software as a service for customer relationship management
Database as a service (DBaaS)

explanation: DBaaS is a managed database in which the provider handles OS and engine patching, backups and availability features while the customer designs schemas and writes SQL. IaaS leaves patching and backups to the customer. Co-located on-premises servers still need the company to manage everything. A SaaS CRM gives an application rather than a database the company can design.

prompt: A sales department subscribes to a hosted CRM application. The DBA is asked to add an index to speed up a slow CRM report. Why is this usually not possible?

options.text: In SaaS the provider manages the application's database, so customers cannot change it directly
CRM data is always stored as unstructured files
SaaS products do not store any data
Indexes cannot be created on tables that contain customer data, because indexing would expose personal information

explanation: With SaaS the customer uses the application while the provider owns and manages the underlying database, so tuning is limited to what the application exposes. CRM data is largely structured, not unstructured files. SaaS products clearly store customer data. Indexes can be created on any table by whoever administers the database; here the customer is simply not that administrator.

prompt: A database running in a container lost all its data when the container was recreated during an update. What should be configured so that the data persists?

options.text: A larger container memory limit
A different container base image
A persistent volume mounted at the database's data directory
More CPU cores for the container host

explanation: A container's writable layer is discarded when the container is replaced, so database files must sit on a persistent volume that outlives the container. More memory or CPU does not change where data is stored. A different base image still writes to an ephemeral layer unless a persistent volume is mounted.

prompt: After migrating a database to a new platform, a DBA compares each table's row count, column names, data types, nullability and default values between the source and the target. Which testing activity is this?

options.text: Stress testing of the application tier
Database quality check of columns and tables
Penetration testing of the database listener
Failover testing of the cluster

explanation: Comparing tables and column definitions, and confirming row counts match, is a quality check that the structure and contents were migrated correctly. Stress testing measures behaviour under extreme load. Penetration testing looks for exploitable security weaknesses. Failover testing confirms that a standby can take over.

prompt: A team plans to rename a column that several applications read. The new release of one application will use the new name, but older applications cannot be updated for two months. Which consideration is this, and what approach handles it?

options.text: Index analysis; drop the old index first
Stress testing; run a load test after the rename
Data sovereignty; move the table to another region so that each application reads a copy under local law
Schema compatibility; keep the old name available through a view or transitional column

explanation: Schema compatibility is about making sure schema changes do not break existing consumers; keeping the old name available through a view or a transitional column lets both versions work. Index analysis concerns whether indexes exist and are used. Stress testing measures performance limits, not compatibility. Data sovereignty concerns the legal location of data.

prompt: Before a holiday sale, a retailer wants to find out how many simultaneous checkout transactions the database can handle before response times exceed the SLA, and how it behaves beyond that point. Which test should be run?

options.text: A stress test that increases load past expected peak levels
A regression test of existing features
A schema compatibility check
A unit test of a single stored procedure

explanation: A stress test drives load up to and past expected peaks to find the breaking point and observe how the system degrades. A regression test checks that existing features still behave correctly after a change. A schema compatibility check looks at structural changes. A unit test checks one component in isolation and says nothing about capacity.

prompt: A database patch has been applied in the test environment. The team reruns a suite of existing test cases covering stored procedures, reports and application transactions to confirm their results are unchanged. What type of testing is this?

options.text: Stress testing
Penetration testing
Regression testing
Capacity projection

explanation: Regression testing reruns existing tests after a change to confirm that previously working functions still give the same results. Stress testing finds performance limits under load. Penetration testing looks for security weaknesses. Capacity projection estimates future resource needs and is not a test of behaviour.

prompt: After loading a migrated database, a DBA wants to confirm that no order lines reference missing orders and that the indexes from the source system exist and are being used by key queries. Which two validation activities address these goals? (Choose two.)

options.text: Referential integrity checks
Stress testing
Index analysis
Gap analysis
Failback testing

explanation: Referential integrity checks find child rows whose parent keys do not exist, and index analysis confirms that the expected indexes are present and used by the execution plans of key queries. Stress testing measures performance under extreme load. Gap analysis compares current and required capabilities during planning. Failback testing concerns returning service to a primary site after a disaster.

prompt: A data architect is meeting business stakeholders to agree which entities (Customer, Order, Product), attributes and relationships the new system needs. No database product has been chosen yet. Which artefact is being produced?

options.text: A physical schema with data types and tablespaces
A logical schema
An execution plan
A backup and recovery runbook

explanation: A logical schema describes entities, attributes and relationships independently of any database product. A physical schema adds product-specific details such as data types, indexes, partitions and storage, which cannot be decided before a product is chosen. An execution plan describes how a query will run. A backup runbook covers recovery steps, not data structure.

prompt: A DBA is turning an approved logical model into a design for PostgreSQL, choosing column data types, primary key implementations, indexes, partitioning of the largest table and tablespace placement. Which schema is being developed?

options.text: Conceptual schema
Logical schema
Physical schema
External view schema

explanation: The physical schema specifies how the design is implemented in a particular database product, including data types, indexes, partitioning and storage placement. A conceptual schema is a high-level business view of the main entities. The logical schema defines entities, attributes and relationships without product-specific details. An external view schema describes what particular users or applications see.

prompt: A DBA moves a large table to a faster tablespace and adds an index, without changing any tables, columns or relationships. Which design documentation needs to be updated?

options.text: The physical schema documentation
The logical schema only
The business glossary only
The conceptual model

explanation: Storage placement and indexes are physical design details, so the physical schema documentation changes while the logical and conceptual models stay the same. The logical schema covers entities, attributes and relationships, which were not altered. A business glossary defines terms, not storage. The conceptual model is a high-level business view.

prompt: New analysts keep misreading the orders.status column, which stores codes such as P, S and X, and do not know which team owns the table. What documentation should the DBA provide?

options.text: An entity relationship diagram showing every table and the relationships between them
A data dictionary listing each column's data type, meaning, allowed values and owner
The database server's error log
A network diagram of the data centre
